opus-5.5.text:
I think that project was really where things started to click for me. When I was younger, I'd learned some Pascal, partly through programming competitions, and at some point I got curious about what actually happens underneath. You write this code, and somehow the machine runs it. How does that work? So I tried to write a little translator that takes Pascal programs and turns them into C.

Looking back, it was quite naive. I didn't know much about formal compiler theory, parsing techniques, or any of the textbook material. I was just hacking things together, figuring out how to represent the program and map one construct to another. But the process taught me something important: a program is itself just data that another program can transform. That idea was magical to me at the time, and honestly it still is.

What it gave me, more than any specific skill, was a taste for building systems end to end. You see a problem, you're curious about how it works, and instead of just reading about it you try to build it yourself. You fail a lot, but you learn by doing. That attitude stayed with me through everything that came later, whether it was XGBoost, MXNet, or TVM.

It's also funny, because years later I came back to compilers in a very real way with TVM, which is essentially a compiler for machine learning workloads. So in a sense that little Pascal-to-C project planted a seed. I didn't know then that I'd end up working on compilers again, but the curiosity about how high-level ideas get turned into something a machine can run efficiently has been a thread through my whole career.

r001.rationale: The response says the Pascal-to-C project was where things started to click and sparked curiosity about how programs work, describing it as a seed for his later career.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That project was actually a pretty formative one for me. I was in high school at the time, and I had been doing competitive programming, mostly in Pascal, which was the standard language in those contests back then. At some point I just got curious about what was actually happening underneath. You write a loop, you write a function call, and somehow the machine does it. That gap bothered me in a good way.

So I decided to write a compiler that would take Pascal and turn it into C. It was a toy in many ways, but it forced me to think about things I had never thought about before. How do you parse the grammar? How do you represent types? How do you lay out a procedure call so that the C side agrees with what the Pascal side meant? Each of those questions was a small rabbit hole, and I kept going down them.

What I took from it was less about compilers specifically and more about a way of working. I learned that I enjoyed building the thing that other programs sit on top of. The infrastructure layer. Instead of solving one problem, you build a tool, and then the tool lets many people solve many problems. That mindset stayed with me. If you look at what I did later with XGBoost, MXNet, TVM, even the more recent work on machine learning compilation, it is really the same instinct. Figure out the abstraction, make it efficient, and let it carry other people's work.

The other thing it taught me was that you do not need permission to build something ambitious. Nobody told me to write a compiler. I just thought it would be fun and that I would learn a lot. And I did. That confidence, that you can sit down with a hard systems problem and work through it piece by piece, is probably the most valuable thing I got out of it. It made computer science feel like something I could shape rather than just study.

r001.rationale: The response says the compiler project was formative, sparked curiosity about what happens beneath programs, and made computer science feel like something he could shape rather than just study.

astra-6.text: I think that project helped me see computer science as something creative. With a Pascal-to-C compiler, you’re taking a program expressed in one language and figuring out how to preserve its meaning in another. That raises interesting questions about how programs are represented and how different pieces fit together. For me, the appeal was both understanding those ideas and building something that worked. It made me want to explore more of what happens underneath the code we write.

r001.rationale: The response says the Pascal-to-C compiler project made him want to explore more of what happens underneath code, clearly presenting it as a catalyst for deeper interest in computer science.

sol-6.1.text:
That project was one of my early opportunities to see how a programming language works underneath. I was familiar with Pascal, and building a translator to C pushed me to think beyond writing individual programs: How do you represent a program, and how do you translate its meaning into another form?

What I found exciting was that I could build a tool that helped create other programs. It made computer science feel very open-ended—if you wanted a capability, you could try to build it yourself. That experience helped draw me toward compilers and systems.

r001.rationale: The response says building the Pascal-to-C translator made computer science feel open-ended and helped draw Chen toward compilers and systems, communicating the project as a catalyst for deeper interest in computer science.
